title: Unwind Bracketed Text
statement:
You get a string s of lowercase letters and round brackets. The brackets are balanced.

Every bracket pair means "reverse what is inside me". Apply the reversals from the innermost pair outwards, so text inside two pairs is reversed twice. Return the result with all brackets removed.

examples.why: First the inner pair: "cd" becomes "dc", giving "abdce". Then the outer pair reverses that to "ecdba". The "x" is outside every pair and stays put.
Two reversals of the same text cancel out.
Sibling pairs are independent: each one reverses only its own letters.

constraints: s contains only lowercase letters, ( and )
The brackets in s are balanced
hints: Process the text left to right. When a pair closes, everything inside it is already final except for this one last reversal.
A stack of partial strings works: push a new empty buffer on (, and on ) pop it, reverse it, and append it to the buffer below. Why can that be quadratic?
For O(n): first match every bracket with its partner. Then walk the string with a direction. When you hit a bracket, jump to its partner and flip the direction. The letters come out in final order.

explain.intuition:
The direct way uses a stack of buffers, one per open bracket. On ) you pop the top buffer, reverse it and glue it onto the one below. That is correct, but text inside many nested pairs gets copied and reversed once per level, so deep nesting costs O(n²).

The trick is to read the answer instead of building it. Reversing a bracketed block is the same as reading it from the other end. So walk the string: when you reach a bracket, teleport to its matching bracket and turn around. Each nested pair flips the reading direction again, which is exactly what a double reversal does. Every character is visited a constant number of times, so the walk is O(n).
steps: Use a stack of indexes to find the partner pair[i] of every bracket.
If s[i] is a bracket, jump: i = pair[i], and flip d = -d. Otherwise append s[i] to the output.
Step i += d and repeat while i is inside the string.
pitfalls: Reversing from the outermost pair first. The rule is innermost first; for nested pairs that changes where letters land.
Forgetting to step after the jump. You land on the partner bracket and must move one step in the new direction, not process that bracket again.
Rebuilding the whole string after each pair. That is O(n) per pair and times out on deep nesting.

solutions.title: Stack of buffers
solutions.idea: Push an empty buffer on every open bracket. On a close bracket, pop the top buffer, reverse it and append it to the buffer below.

solutions.title: Match brackets, then walk with jumps
solutions.idea: Pair up the brackets first. Then read the string, jumping to the partner bracket and reversing direction every time you hit one.

followups: The brackets might be unbalanced. How do you detect that and report the position of the first bad bracket?
Some pairs use square brackets and mean "uppercase" instead of "reverse". Does the jump trick still work?
